questions.title: Testing practice 1
questions.prompt: Which input is the best boundary case for a function that finds the largest list item?
choices: A list with one item
A list with ten random items
The same three-item list twice
A list already used in the demo
questions.explanation: One item is the smallest valid list for this function. It checks whether the code wrongly assumes that a second item exists.

questions.title: Testing practice 2
questions.prompt: What happens when an assert expression is false?
choices: Python raises AssertionError
Python changes 5 to 4
The line is ignored
Python returns False from the program
questions.explanation: An assert statement stops at a false condition and raises AssertionError. Test tools catch that error and show which expectation failed.

questions.title: Trace Testing
questions.code:
def is_even(number):
    return number % 2 == 0

assert is_even(4) is True
assert is_even(7) is False
print("checks passed")
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Each assertion states one expectation. If an expression is false, Python raises AssertionError and points to the failed check. The resulting output is 'checks passed'.

questions.title: Testing practice 5
questions.prompt: Why is `assert total([2, 3, 5]) == 10` a better test than `assert total(nums) == sum(x for x in nums)`?
choices: It checks a known expected value instead of recomputing the answer a second way
assert cannot compare against sum()
The second version does not compile
10 is faster to compare than a generator
questions.explanation: A good test states the answer you expect (10) so a reader can see at a glance what correct means. Recomputing the result with `sum(...)` just tests two implementations against each other, and both could share the same bug. The second line runs fine; the issue is that it verifies less.

questions.title: One passing test
questions.prompt: Why can a function still be buggy after one test passes?
choices: One test proves only the case it checks.
Passing one test means the function was not actually run.
A passing test always hides syntax errors.
Python tests work only when every input is positive.
questions.explanation: A single passing case gives useful evidence, but it is narrow evidence. If every test uses ordinary positive numbers, bugs around empty input, zero, duplicates, or negative values may stay hidden. Add cases that represent the range of behavior you care about.

questions.title: Focused tests
questions.prompt: What makes a test failure easier to understand?
choices: Check many unrelated behaviors in one assert.
Test one clear behavior with a direct expected result.
Use random expected values so failures are surprising.
Avoid naming the behavior being tested.
questions.explanation: When a test checks one behavior, a failure points to a specific rule. If a test combines too many ideas, you may know something failed but not what. Clear inputs, clear expected output, and a focused name make the test more useful.

questions.title: Expected results
questions.prompt: A test checks `total([2, 3, 5])`. What expected value should it compare against?
choices: `total([2, 3, 5])`, because comparing the function to itself is enough.
`sum(x for x in nums)`, even if `nums` is not shown in the test.
`10`, because the expected result is fixed and easy to verify by hand.
`None`, because tests should not know the answer.
questions.explanation: A good test uses an expected value that is independent of the function being tested. `10` is obvious from the input and does not repeat the same logic. Recomputing the expected answer with similar code can copy the same bug into the test.

questions.title: Boundary cases
questions.prompt: A function finds the largest number in a list. Which test set gives better coverage?
choices: Only `[3, 8, 2]`, because one normal list is enough.
Only `[100]`, because short inputs cover every case.
Only `[1, 2, 3]`, because sorted input is easiest.
A normal list, a one-item list, and a list with negative numbers.
questions.explanation: Normal examples are important, but boundaries reveal different bugs. A one-item list checks the smallest non-empty shape, and negative numbers catch code that starts with an unsafe default such as 0. Coverage means choosing cases for the rules that could break.

questions.title: Readable test names
questions.prompt: Which test name best communicates its purpose?
choices: `test_total_handles_empty_list`
`test1`
`check_stuff`
`temporary_test_do_not_use`
questions.explanation: A test name should say what behavior is being protected. When `test_total_handles_empty_list` fails, the reader immediately knows which case needs attention. Vague names force extra digging before the failure is useful.

questions.title: Rerunning tests
questions.prompt: After changing a helper function used in several places, what should happen next?
choices: Run only the one example that was edited by hand.
Run the relevant tests again to catch new breakage.
Delete old tests because the code has changed.
Assume unchanged files cannot be affected.
questions.explanation: A helper can affect callers you did not touch directly. Rerunning the relevant tests checks both the intended fix and possible side effects. This habit turns tests into a safety net instead of a one-time assignment.
